These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase. ## Preferences - **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does. - **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`. - **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc. - **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control. - **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.) - **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of. - **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes. - **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked. # Claudinite — active-pack guidance The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand. # Working discipline The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project. Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better. Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. 1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule. 2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes. 3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it. The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for. Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided. When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs. When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix." Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out. Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere. Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet. When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change. An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action. # The task lifecycle The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill. For every new task: 1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work. 2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`). 3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done. --- # HTML Portable, project-agnostic practices for hand-authored HTML — semantic markup, accessibility, forms, and the document structure pitfalls that recur regardless of framework — true for any HTML read cold. - **Injected block markup inside a `

` silently empties it — read the sibling, not the tag.** When a `

` is filled with raw HTML (e.g. `innerHTML`, or a framework's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html` / `ng-bind-html`), a block element inside it (a `

`, etc.) is disallowed by the HTML content model, so the parser (browser or jsdom, same rule) auto-closes the `

` right before it and the injected content lands as the `

`'s **next sibling**. Read `element.nextElementSibling`. - **An ambiguous numeric slash date can't be resolved from its digits — infer the document's convention once, don't guess per-field.** When both parts are ≤ 12 (e.g. `05/07/2026`), resolve the order once per document — never per source or per field — in this order. (1) **An unambiguous sibling date fixes the page's convention**: a slash date elsewhere on the same page with a part > 12 (e.g. `24/07/2026`) parses only one way, and a page is almost always internally consistent — read that date's order and apply it to every other slash date on the page. (2) Failing that, **read the declared locale** (``, `og:locale`): default **month-first** (the order `Date` and most JS parsers assume) and flip to day-first only on a *positive* non-US signal — a non-US region in `lang` / `og:locale`, or a non-English language; a bare `en` with unknown region stays month-first. The `.` / `-` separators are day-first regardless. - **When code must react to how a real page actually behaves, investigate it live before you ship — don't deploy a hypothesis you can only test after release.** If a change hinges on the real DOM, computed styles, or runtime state of a page you can't see, hand the user one JavaScript snippet to run in the browser DevTools console and read its output back. Reserve "test it after it's deployed" for behavior you've verified genuinely can't be observed now. - **Make that console request a snippet, not an essay.** Send exactly one code block to paste into the console and ask the user to paste its output back. Skip the prose explaining what you're hoping to learn. --- # product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in place). Layout, required page sections, the Key insights header's shape, growth-log dating, source links, staleness, and the isolation wall are **check-enforced** — the finding is the instruction, so this prose never restates them. The full growth procedure is the pack's task doc (`packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.md`). - **Every page opens with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a few bullets carrying the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the competitor that already does this, the thing that turned out not to be true — enough that a human who reads only the header understands what was researched and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing and competitors"), not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to. - **Terse, plain, and only the non-obvious.** One short line per bullet, in ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would *surprise* someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the number nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point is obvious is genuinely hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep it**. A borderline-obvious line costs the reader two seconds; a long, careful line costs them the header. - **The header is a current view, not a log.** A pass that changes what a page's most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded insight leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below), and an insight the pass didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's top-line understanding, the header doesn't move. - **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may build on. - **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass. Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current. - **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source), never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's growth log and updates the open questions in both directions. - **No fabricated growth.** Most passes find little or nothing; no new citable material → no edit, no log entry, no PR. - **sample-data and new wikis.** `product-wiki/sample-data/` gains a file only when a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test asserts against belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/` outside the two reserved names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so create one only deliberately, seeded with its required sections; automation refines existing pages, it never invents new ones. - **Review discipline.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR — researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate. The owner phrase **"grow the product wiki"** runs the worker method in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR discipline. --- # tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills ([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md), [single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md), [single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)). The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.** - **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete; **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a ref's auto-generated name. - **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive. Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites **its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body. --- # repo-mechanics — rules ## A step only the owner can perform goes in its own issue, never in the PR body A merged PR's body is not a to-do list anyone returns to. PR #12 shipped the Pages deploy with its one-time setup — *"in the repo's Settings → Pages, set the source to GitHub Actions"* — as a Notes bullet in the PR description. It merged, the note went with it, and two days later issue #40 had to re-file that exact setting, still unticked, alongside the rest of the pipeline's manual settings. PR #2 did the same with two adoption leftovers in a review comment. So: when a change lands something that cannot work until a human flips a repository setting (Pages source, workflow permissions, a repo variable, a deployment-environment rule), open an **issue** for it — a checkbox per setting, each saying what breaks while it is off, and a stated closing condition — and link it from the PR. Keep the note in the PR too if you like, but the issue is the thing that survives the merge. The exception is a step whose home is an artifact the owner is already editing (the executor routine carries its own leftovers in its prompt, per bootstrap); anywhere else, an issue. And before handing a step over at all, check you actually can't do it — see the `session-tooling` rule on searching a tool's literal name. ## Check the canon packs before hand-authoring release or CI plumbing PR #31 hand-rolled this repo's release: `scripts/bump-version.mjs` plus a version-bump-and-push step in `deploy-pages.yml`, adopting the scheme by copying what a sibling fleet repo already ran. Within a day, issue #38 and PR #39 deleted all of it — script, bump step, workflow, and the separate `checks.yml` — for the vendored `static-website` pack, which owns the same pipeline as a standard with its own checks over it. The tell was there when it was written: **a mechanic being copied from another repo in the fleet is a canon candidate, not a file to author here.** The second copy is the moment to raise it centrally, because a bespoke third copy gets thrown away and takes its reviewed workflow, its version scheme and its CI entry with it. So before writing release, deploy, versioning or CI wiring in this repo, look for the pack that owns it; if none does and a sibling repo already solved it, that's the finding to report, not the code to duplicate. --- # session-tooling — rules ## Never use WebFetch to obtain content you must have `WebFetch` fails two different ways in this environment, and both were paid for in one session: - **It summarizes.** Asked for "the complete verbatim content" of a raw `githubusercontent.com` file, it returned a prose description of the document instead. The file had to be re-fetched with `curl -sSL -o /f.md ` and read from disk — the correct move the first time. - **It 403s.** Four consecutive fetches of ordinary publisher pages (`gartner.com`, `fortunebusinessinsights.com`, `marketdataforecast.com`, `squarerootseo.com`) all returned `403 Forbidden`, so a research pass ended up attributing figures to search snippets instead of verifying them at source. So: when the content itself matters, `curl` it into the scratchpad and `Read` it. When a page 403s, do **not** retry it or try a sibling URL — take the `WebSearch` snippet, attribute it to the publisher rather than asserting it, and flag it for re-verification. `WebSearch` itself works fine and is the right first reach. **`codeload.github.com` is blocked here too** — `curl … | tar -xz` of a repo tarball returns 403. Use `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com//`, which works through the proxy and yields the same tree. ## A ToolSearch that finds nothing does not mean the tool is absent Deferred tools are matched by keyword, and the keywords are not the tool's own vocabulary. A session searched `"create trigger routine scheduled task automation"`, got back `TaskCreate`/`CronCreate`/etc., concluded there was no trigger API in the session, and told the owner to create a scheduled routine by hand — while `create_trigger` was in its tool list the whole time. The owner's reply was "Why didn't you create the routine? You should have." Before telling the owner a step is theirs because the capability is missing: search the **literal name** (`select:create_trigger`), and try the tool. A negative keyword search is evidence about the query, not about the environment — and handing the owner work the session could have done is the expensive half of the mistake. **`select:` wants the fully-qualified name — for an MCP tool that means the `mcp____` prefix.** `select:issue_read`, `select:pull_request_read` and `select:enable_pr_auto_merge` each return `No matching deferred tools found`, which reads exactly like an absent tool; `select:mcp__github__issue_read` returns it. Three executor sessions on 2026-08-01 hit this six times between them (two in session `1fc538f6`, three in `ecc58551`, one in `000d1bf8`), every one recovered by a second `ToolSearch` — ~2–4s and a wasted call each, and the usual recovery (fall back to a keyword query) pulls back five to ten schemas where the `select:` would have pulled one. Copy the prefix off the deferred-tools list rather than typing the short name from memory. ## `Edit` needs the `Read` tool — `cat`/`grep`/`sed` do not count Inspecting a file through Bash does **not** register it as read. A session that had just explored a freshly-cloned repo with `cat`, `grep -n` and `tail` went straight to `Edit` on three of those files and got `File has not been read yet. Read it first before writing to it.` three times in a row (23:25:07, 23:25:09, 23:25:15) before backing off to `Read` and retrying — ~17s and four wasted calls for zero information gained, since the file contents were already on screen from the shell. The trap is specific to **exploring with the shell and then editing**, which is the natural rhythm when surveying an unfamiliar tree (a second repo cloned into the session, a vendored directory). So: the moment shell output tells you a file is the one you're going to change, `Read` that exact path before the first `Edit`. Reading a targeted `offset`/`limit` window is enough — the precondition is the tool call, not the byte count. ## `enable_pr_auto_merge` cannot be armed in this repo — don't retry it `main` carries **no branch-protection rule**, and GitHub only offers auto-merge on a protected branch. Every task that says "open the PR and arm auto-merge" will fail here until an owner adds one. Worse, the *first* refusal lies about why. One run got `The pull request is in unstable status (required checks are failing)` at 05:11:52 while the `Claudinite world sweep` check was merely still **queued** — it went green moments later. The agent believed the message, re-checked, retried at 05:12:19, and only then got the real error: `Protected branch rules not configured for this branch`. ~50s of retries, a tracker comment that had to be corrected by a second comment, and an otherwise completely successful run converged as `needs-human`. So: **do not treat "required checks are failing" from `enable_pr_auto_merge` as a check failure** — read `pull_request_read` `get_check_runs` and look at `status`, not `conclusion`. And do not retry the arm: one refusal mentioning branch protection is final. When the task's own spec authorizes landing without human review (the growth tasks do), poll `get_check_runs` until the required check *completes* successfully and then `merge_pull_request` with `squash`. Escalate `needs-human` only when the task requires a reviewer. ## A scheduled executor turn still needs a `Comment class:` line The `comment-classification` check treats the scheduler's launch prompt (`Execute the Claudinite executor: …`) as the owner's latest comment, so **every** unattended executor session is one blocking Stop-hook finding away from ending. It fired in all three executor sessions captured on 2026-07-31, without exception. Knowing this costs 7–11 seconds (emit the line, stop again). *Not* knowing it cost one session over two minutes of reading `comment-classification.mjs`, `helpers/work.mjs` and `helpers/repo-context.mjs` to work out why an automated dispatch was being judged as conversation. So: when the session's opening prompt is a scheduler dispatch, put `Comment class: other` in your **first** substantive reply — a command phrase is `other` by the rule's own wording. Don't wait for the Stop hook to tell you. ## A subagent shares your working tree — put the branch back before you stop `Agent` subagents run in the *same* checkout, not a worktree of their own. A subagent that does `git checkout` to reach a PR branch silently moves the parent, and the parent's Stop hook then evaluates commits that aren't the parent's. One executor sat on its own branch, dispatched a baselining subagent that checked out `claudinite/maintenance-2026-07-31-e7xiad`, and got `task-lifecycle: none of the 1 commit(s) since origin/main references an issue (#N)` about a commit written by preprocessing, not by it. Two blocked Stop rounds and ~2m40s of investigation (05:09:46 → 05:12:25); the fix was one `git checkout` back to its own branch, after which the hook passed unchanged. So: after any subagent that may touch git, run `git branch --show-current` and switch back before ending the turn — and read a surprising `task-lifecycle` finding as "am I on the branch I think I'm on?" before reading it as a real lifecycle violation. ## The mounted `.claudinite/shared/` is code without its docs — and its runners are silent when clean Two ways the engine mount misleads a session that goes reading it, both paid for on 2026-08-01: - **The `DESIGN.md` it cites is not vendored here.** Engine source refers to it constantly (`// World-scope conformance runner (see DESIGN.md)`, `// … (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §1, §5.5)`), but `find .claudinite -iname 'DESIGN*'` returns nothing — the mount carries `.mjs` and pack docs only. Session `000d1bf8` chased it twice independently: the executor spent 05:00:52→05:01:00 on a failed `Read` plus two `find`s, then its subagent repeated the same hunt at 05:02:23→05:02:26. ~25s and five calls for a file that was never there. Read the module header comment instead — it restates what the missing section would have said. - **A clean check run prints nothing at all.** `check_the_world.mjs` on a green repo emits zero output and exits `0`; `report-findings.mjs` only prints when there are findings. Session `055f2992` had `EXIT:0` in hand at 05:01:40 and still spent 05:01:42→05:02:12 — four more calls, `--help`, `head`, `tail`, `grep`, a full `Read` — confirming that silence meant success. So: when the engine's own comments point at a doc, check it exists before hunting for it, and re-run a runner with `; echo "EXIT:$?"` **once** — the exit code is the whole answer, and no output is the good outcome. ## Never publish an unverified fact about a real person When the primary source for a person's background is blocked, **do not substitute a data broker, and do not publish the claim with a caveat** — ask the owner. A session needed the founder's career history for the site's who-we-are section. `WebFetch` of his LinkedIn profile returned `403`, so the pass fell back to `WebSearch` and wrote employers and a degree onto a public marketing page from third-party aggregator listings, flagging the paragraph for the owner to sanity-check. The owner's reply: *"zoominfo is wrong and rocketreach doesn't add anything"* — the facts were wrong, and the page had already shipped in a PR. Stripping them cost a second commit and an amended requirement. Flagging is not a substitute for verification here, because the cost is not a wrong paragraph — it is a public claim about a named person that they never made. The person is in the conversation; one question is cheaper than any research. (The site-specific form of this now sits in `product-wiki/product-requirements/` as a reviewed requirement; this rule is the general one, for any repo and any surface.) --- # site-copy — rules ## When a change adds or alters tracking/data-collection behavior, update the claims that describe it in the same commit PR #20 added Cloudflare Web Analytics (visit counting) and shipped `privacy.html` in the same commit — but the page's first draft still led with *"no cookies, no tracking, no personal data,"* a claim the very commit adding it had just made false. 23	
24	For each rule, ask the one question from
25	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
26	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
27	
28	- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
29	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
30	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
31	  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
32	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.
33	
34	The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
35	part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.

38	
39	Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
40	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:
41	
42	1. **Author the check** in the owning pack (`<pack>/<rule>.mjs`, listed in its `pack.mjs`) — the
43	   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).
44	2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
45	   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
46	   doesn't ship.
47	3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory only when the rule is
48	   directional by kind.
49	4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
50	   how you decide which paragraphs those are.
51	
52	**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
53	its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
54	which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's

56	check to the same fixture bar.

59	candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.

62

64	deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
65	paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent

17	consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by default — projects don't
18	improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core `packs/`. Read the
19	prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them). Never edit a
20	read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.
21	
22	## What to look for — the check-the-world test
23	
24	For each rule, ask the one question from
25	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
26	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
27	
28	- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
29	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
30	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
31	  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
32	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.
33	
34	The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
35	part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.
36	
37	## How to convert one
38	
39	Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
40	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:
41	
42	1. **Author the check** in the owning pack (`<pack>/<rule>.mjs`, listed in its `pack.mjs`) — the
43	   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).
44	2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
45	   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
46	   doesn't ship.
47	3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory only when the rule is
48	   directional by kind.
49	4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
50	   how you decide which paragraphs those are.
51	
52	**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
53	its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
54	which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
55	*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
56	check to the same fixture bar.
57	
58	When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
59	candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.
60	
61	## Coming out: the deletion test
62	
63	Coming out of a conversion, apply the **deletion test**: prose a mechanism fully covers is
64	deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
65	paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent
66	how to fix it?* If yes, it is redundant: delete it whole. The check's failure message is where
67	the rule lives now and its header comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating
68	either pays twice and is the drift trap waiting to spring.
69	
70	Before concluding prose is the only carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an
71	activity-scoped skill often already holds the map a rule is repeating. Keep only what no artifact
72	carries.
73	
74	The test **discriminates** rather than just deleting: a paragraph stays whole whenever it carries
75	something the check does not — a second rule in the same breath, an exemption the check can't
76	encode, a value the check can't judge, or a remedy the finding's own `fix` line never states
77	(a finding renders `what` / `why` / `fix` / `doc`, never the rule's `description`, so a remedy
78	that lives only in the description is not carried). Two worked calls: an `npm test` invariant
79	went entirely — the check caught it and the testing-guide skill already listed the suites —
80	while an `extension-test/` mirror bullet stayed, because the check beside it enforced only the
81	`package.json` list's sync with the tree and never the mirror convention itself.
82	
83	Whether a check covers a rule is a judgment about meaning, so this test is applied by a
84	**reader**, not mechanized.
85	
86	## Bounds
87	
88	- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
89	  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
90	- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — the deletion test is only ever asked of a rule a
91	  *landed* check now enforces.
92	- Run the suite and the sweep green before opening the PR; open it for the owner's approval,
93	  never a direct push to `main`.

1	# repo-mechanics — rules
2	
3	## A step only the owner can perform goes in its own issue, never in the PR body
4	
5	A merged PR's body is not a to-do list anyone returns to. PR #12 shipped the
6	Pages deploy with its one-time setup — *"in the repo's Settings → Pages, set the
7	source to GitHub Actions"* — as a Notes bullet in the PR description. It merged,
8	the note went with it, and two days later issue #40 had to re-file that exact
9	setting, still unticked, alongside the rest of the pipeline's manual settings.
10	PR #2 did the same with two adoption leftovers in a review comment.
11	
12	So: when a change lands something that cannot work until a human flips a
13	repository setting (Pages source, workflow permissions, a repo variable, a
14	deployment-environment rule), open an **issue** for it — a checkbox per setting,
15	each saying what breaks while it is off, and a stated closing condition — and
16	link it from the PR. Keep the note in the PR too if you like, but the issue is
17	the thing that survives the merge. The exception is a step whose home is an
18	artifact the owner is already editing (the executor routine carries its own
19	leftovers in its prompt, per bootstrap); anywhere else, an issue.
20	
21	And before handing a step over at all, check you actually can't do it — see the
22	`session-tooling` rule on searching a tool's literal name.
23	
24	## Check the canon packs before hand-authoring release or CI plumbing
25	
26	PR #31 hand-rolled this repo's release: `scripts/bump-version.mjs` plus a
27	version-bump-and-push step in `deploy-pages.yml`, adopting the scheme by copying
28	what a sibling fleet repo already ran. Within a day, issue #38 and PR #39
29	deleted all of it — script, bump step, workflow, and the separate `checks.yml` —
30	for the vendored `static-website` pack, which owns the same pipeline as a
31	standard with its own checks over it.
32	
33	The tell was there when it was written: **a mechanic being copied from another
34	repo in the fleet is a canon candidate, not a file to author here.** The second
35	copy is the moment to raise it centrally, because a bespoke third copy gets
36	thrown away and takes its reviewed workflow, its version scheme and its CI entry
37	with it. So before writing release, deploy, versioning or CI wiring in this
38	repo, look for the pack that owns it; if none does and a sibling repo already
39	solved it, that's the finding to report, not the code to duplicate.

1	# session-tooling — rules
2	
3	## Never use WebFetch to obtain content you must have
4	
5	`WebFetch` fails two different ways in this environment, and both were paid for in
6	one session:
7	
8	- **It summarizes.** Asked for "the complete verbatim content" of a raw
9	  `githubusercontent.com` file, it returned a prose description of the document
10	  instead. The file had to be re-fetched with `curl -sSL -o <scratch>/f.md <url>`
11	  and read from disk — the correct move the first time.
12	- **It 403s.** Four consecutive fetches of ordinary publisher pages
13	  (`gartner.com`, `fortunebusinessinsights.com`, `marketdataforecast.com`,
14	  `squarerootseo.com`) all returned `403 Forbidden`, so a research pass ended up
15	  attributing figures to search snippets instead of verifying them at source.
16	
17	So: when the content itself matters, `curl` it into the scratchpad and `Read` it.
18	When a page 403s, do **not** retry it or try a sibling URL — take the `WebSearch`
19	snippet, attribute it to the publisher rather than asserting it, and flag it for
20	re-verification. `WebSearch` itself works fine and is the right first reach.
21	
22	**`codeload.github.com` is blocked here too** — `curl … | tar -xz` of a repo
23	tarball returns 403. Use `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>`,
24	which works through the proxy and yields the same tree.
25	
26	## A ToolSearch that finds nothing does not mean the tool is absent
27	
28	Deferred tools are matched by keyword, and the keywords are not the tool's own
29	vocabulary. A session searched `"create trigger routine scheduled task
30	automation"`, got back `TaskCreate`/`CronCreate`/etc., concluded there was no
31	trigger API in the session, and told the owner to create a scheduled routine by
32	hand — while `create_trigger` was in its tool list the whole time. The owner's
33	reply was "Why didn't you create the routine? You should have."
34	
35	Before telling the owner a step is theirs because the capability is missing:
36	search the **literal name** (`select:create_trigger`), and try the tool. A
37	negative keyword search is evidence about the query, not about the environment —
38	and handing the owner work the session could have done is the expensive half of
39	the mistake.
40	
41	**`select:` wants the fully-qualified name — for an MCP tool that means the
42	`mcp__<server>__` prefix.** `select:issue_read`, `select:pull_request_read` and
43	`select:enable_pr_auto_merge` each return `No matching deferred tools found`,
44	which reads exactly like an absent tool; `select:mcp__github__issue_read` returns
45	it. Three executor sessions on 2026-08-01 hit this six times between them (two in
46	session `1fc538f6`, three in `ecc58551`, one in `000d1bf8`), every one recovered
47	by a second `ToolSearch` — ~2–4s and a wasted call each, and the usual recovery
48	(fall back to a keyword query) pulls back five to ten schemas where the `select:`
49	would have pulled one. Copy the prefix off the deferred-tools list rather than
50	typing the short name from memory.
51	
52	## `Edit` needs the `Read` tool — `cat`/`grep`/`sed` do not count
53	
54	Inspecting a file through Bash does **not** register it as read. A session that had
55	just explored a freshly-cloned repo with `cat`, `grep -n` and `tail` went straight to
56	`Edit` on three of those files and got
57	`<tool_use_error>File has not been read yet. Read it first before writing to it.</tool_use_error>`
58	three times in a row (23:25:07, 23:25:09, 23:25:15) before backing off to `Read` and
59	retrying — ~17s and four wasted calls for zero information gained, since the file
60	contents were already on screen from the shell.
61	
62	The trap is specific to **exploring with the shell and then editing**, which is the
63	natural rhythm when surveying an unfamiliar tree (a second repo cloned into the
64	session, a vendored directory). So: the moment shell output tells you a file is the
65	one you're going to change, `Read` that exact path before the first `Edit`. Reading a
66	targeted `offset`/`limit` window is enough — the precondition is the tool call, not
67	the byte count.
68	
69	## `enable_pr_auto_merge` cannot be armed in this repo — don't retry it
70	
71	`main` carries **no branch-protection rule**, and GitHub only offers auto-merge on a
72	protected branch. Every task that says "open the PR and arm auto-merge" will fail here
73	until an owner adds one.
74	
75	Worse, the *first* refusal lies about why. One run got
76	`The pull request is in unstable status (required checks are failing)` at 05:11:52 while
77	the `Claudinite world sweep` check was merely still **queued** — it went green moments
78	later. The agent believed the message, re-checked, retried at 05:12:19, and only then got
79	the real error: `Protected branch rules not configured for this branch`. ~50s of retries,
80	a tracker comment that had to be corrected by a second comment, and an otherwise
81	completely successful run converged as `needs-human`.
82	
83	So: **do not treat "required checks are failing" from `enable_pr_auto_merge` as a check
84	failure** — read `pull_request_read` `get_check_runs` and look at `status`, not
85	`conclusion`. And do not retry the arm: one refusal mentioning branch protection is
86	final. When the task's own spec authorizes landing without human review (the growth
87	tasks do), poll `get_check_runs` until the required check *completes* successfully and
88	then `merge_pull_request` with `squash`. Escalate `needs-human` only when the task
89	requires a reviewer.
90	
91	## A scheduled executor turn still needs a `Comment class:` line
92	
93	The `comment-classification` check treats the scheduler's launch prompt
94	(`Execute the Claudinite executor: …`) as the owner's latest comment, so **every**
95	unattended executor session is one blocking Stop-hook finding away from ending. It fired
96	in all three executor sessions captured on 2026-07-31, without exception.
97	
98	Knowing this costs 7–11 seconds (emit the line, stop again). *Not* knowing it cost one
99	session over two minutes of reading `comment-classification.mjs`, `helpers/work.mjs` and
100	`helpers/repo-context.mjs` to work out why an automated dispatch was being judged as
101	conversation.
102	
103	So: when the session's opening prompt is a scheduler dispatch, put
104	`Comment class: other` in your **first** substantive reply — a command phrase is `other`
105	by the rule's own wording. Don't wait for the Stop hook to tell you.
106	
107	## A subagent shares your working tree — put the branch back before you stop
108	
109	`Agent` subagents run in the *same* checkout, not a worktree of their own. A subagent that
110	does `git checkout` to reach a PR branch silently moves the parent, and the parent's Stop
111	hook then evaluates commits that aren't the parent's.
112	
113	One executor sat on its own branch, dispatched a baselining subagent that checked out
114	`claudinite/maintenance-2026-07-31-e7xiad`, and got
115	`task-lifecycle: none of the 1 commit(s) since origin/main references an issue (#N)`
116	about a commit written by preprocessing, not by it. Two blocked Stop rounds and ~2m40s of
117	investigation (05:09:46 → 05:12:25); the fix was one `git checkout` back to its own
118	branch, after which the hook passed unchanged.
119	
120	So: after any subagent that may touch git, run `git branch --show-current` and switch back
121	before ending the turn — and read a surprising `task-lifecycle` finding as "am I on the
122	branch I think I'm on?" before reading it as a real lifecycle violation.
123	
124	## The mounted `.claudinite/shared/` is code without its docs — and its runners are silent when clean
125	
126	Two ways the engine mount misleads a session that goes reading it, both paid for
127	on 2026-08-01:
128	
129	- **The `DESIGN.md` it cites is not vendored here.** Engine source refers to it
130	  constantly (`// World-scope conformance runner (see DESIGN.md)`,
131	  `// … (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §1, §5.5)`), but
132	  `find .claudinite -iname 'DESIGN*'` returns nothing — the mount carries
133	  `.mjs` and pack docs only. Session `000d1bf8` chased it twice independently:
134	  the executor spent 05:00:52→05:01:00 on a failed `Read` plus two `find`s, then
135	  its subagent repeated the same hunt at 05:02:23→05:02:26. ~25s and five calls
136	  for a file that was never there. Read the module header comment instead — it
137	  restates what the missing section would have said.
138	- **A clean check run prints nothing at all.** `check_the_world.mjs` on a green
139	  repo emits zero output and exits `0`; `report-findings.mjs` only prints when
140	  there are findings. Session `055f2992` had `EXIT:0` in hand at 05:01:40 and
141	  still spent 05:01:42→05:02:12 — four more calls, `--help`, `head`, `tail`,
142	  `grep`, a full `Read` — confirming that silence meant success.
143	
144	So: when the engine's own comments point at a doc, check it exists before
145	hunting for it, and re-run a runner with `; echo "EXIT:$?"` **once** — the exit
146	code is the whole answer, and no output is the good outcome.
147	
148	## Never publish an unverified fact about a real person
149	
150	When the primary source for a person's background is blocked, **do not substitute a
151	data broker, and do not publish the claim with a caveat** — ask the owner.
152	
153	A session needed the founder's career history for the site's who-we-are section.
154	`WebFetch` of his LinkedIn profile returned `403`, so the pass fell back to `WebSearch`
155	and wrote employers and a degree onto a public marketing page from third-party
156	aggregator listings, flagging the paragraph for the owner to sanity-check. The owner's
157	reply: *"zoominfo is wrong and rocketreach doesn't add anything"* — the facts were
158	wrong, and the page had already shipped in a PR. Stripping them cost a second commit
159	and an amended requirement.
160	
161	Flagging is not a substitute for verification here, because the cost is not a wrong
162	paragraph — it is a public claim about a named person that they never made. The person
163	is in the conversation; one question is cheaper than any research. (The site-specific
164	form of this now sits in `product-wiki/product-requirements/` as a reviewed
165	requirement; this rule is the general one, for any repo and any surface.)
166

1	# site-copy — rules
2	
3	## When a change adds or alters tracking/data-collection behavior, update the claims that describe it in the same commit
4	
5	PR #20 added Cloudflare Web Analytics (visit counting) and shipped `privacy.html`
6	in the same commit — but the page's first draft still led with *"no cookies, no
7	tracking, no personal data,"* a claim the very commit adding it had just made
8	false. Review caught it before merge: the lede was rewritten to state what's
9	actually measured first, plainly say the site is **not** analytics-free, and keep
10	the narrower claims (no cross-site tracking, no ads, no cookies set by us) only
11	where they remain true.
12	
13	So: treat any existing claim about tracking, data collection, or "what we don't
14	do" as part of the same change that touches that behavior — read `privacy.html`
15	(and the footer/marketing copy that references it) before shipping, and update it
16	in the same commit rather than leaving it for a review round-trip. Lead with what
17	is actually done, then the narrower true claims — never a blanket denial the new
18	behavior no longer supports.

# The repo's check flow — the deterministic place the whole-repo Claudinite
# world sweep runs at each change. The site is static and has no test suite of
# its own yet; when it gains one, add it as a step ahead of the sweep rather
# than as a separate workflow, so one red flow means one thing.
#
# The WORK scope is deliberately absent here: it judges a session's own change
# with that session's transcript and runs at the Stop hook, not in CI.
name: Checks

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  checks:
    name: Claudinite world sweep
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'

      # The engine's always-vendored Node CLI, invoked as the standalone
      # command — never as a language-specific test file a runner discovers.
      - name: Claudinite world scope
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs

1	# Extracting lessons from a working session
2	
3	> **Scope: a single agent ↔ user conversation.** This doc is the **method** for mining one
4	> working session's *dialogue and the actions taken in it* for improvements. It is **not** the
5	> growth extract ([the growth-extract task](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) that mines **issues, PRs, and commits** over repo
6	> history — that routine never sees a conversation. Its two callers: the
7	> [conversation-extract daily task](tasks/conversation-extract/task.md), which applies it to **captured**
8	> conversation logs — where the friction signals below (a clarifying round-trip, a backtrack, a
9	> wait you sat through) survive with their timestamps — and an owner's occasional plain-words
10	> ask for a retrospective over the live session.
11	
12	Portable guidance for mining an agent ↔ user session — a Claude Code web session, a CLI run, a
13	captured conversation log — for durable improvements: read the conversation and convert its
14	friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less dependent on human
15	feedback.
16	
17	Run the reflection on a **capable model.** Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears
18	the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong
19	"lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
20	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model
21	to the judgment it must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the
22	separate efficiency analysis — also live there; this doc is the how-to.
23	
24	## The goal
25	
26	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less
27	rework, less waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but
28	as "where did this cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost
29	next time." If a pass can't name a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's
30	fine (see [No new lessons](#no-new-lessons-is-a-valid--and-common--result)).
31	
32	## When it runs
33	
34	Routinely, in the [conversation-extract daily task](tasks/conversation-extract/task.md) over each captured
35	log (a fresh pass within a day of capture, a final hindsight pass before retention deletes the
36	log) — the standard path. If an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective over the live
37	session, apply the same method and deliver the capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**,
38	never one that self-merges (the nightly auto-merges its own PR per its own doc; a live retrospective
39	wants human eyes). **Never
40	reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner
41	decides when a session is done enough to mine.
42	
43	## What to look for — the friction signals
44	
45	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop
46	cost more than necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
47	
48	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
49	
50	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I
51	meant…"); the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same
52	request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
53	
54	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every
55	question the user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate
56	**convention or glossary entry**; a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first
57	checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc the agent reads cold and gets right the first
58	time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds correctly **without the round-trip**.
59	
60	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
61	
62	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran
63	a command that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light
64	one fit; reinvented something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written
65	to "verify"; missed an existing convention and had it corrected in review.
66	
67	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing
68	helper/convention so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read.** Place
69	it by where the trap is hit, not in a central bucket: a gotcha from **misusing a specific API,
70	class, or library goes as a comment right at the usage site** — next to the call itself, where
71	the next editor of that line sees it — never collected into a centralized gotchas list.
72	Co-locate it in a file's own header comment when the trap spans the whole file and you'd only
73	hit it *while editing that file*. Reserve a central gotchas doc for what no single usage site
74	owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant file (a mistake of omission), or a
75	cross-cutting invariant. The test: next time the agent takes the good path first, not after a
76	detour.
77	
78	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
79	
80	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been
81	parallel; a padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its
82	result was already in hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already
83	green.
84	
85	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers and separate the
86	kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting** (sleeps,
87	polling, a finished process not yet killed). A captured log carries per-entry timestamps and
88	per-message token usage, so the numbers are computable, not estimated. A fix is only credible
89	against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
90	was already optimal.
91	
92	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
93	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the
94	subject of the standing **efficiency analysis** in
95	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold a wall-time
96	finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
97	loss of quality.
98	
99	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
100	
101	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks
102	*repeatedly* are a checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how
103	many processes ran — could it be fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its
104	work was done?", stop waiting to be asked — fold those exact questions into a **standing
105	self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the relevant work, and close with a
106	terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each recurring question
107	converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
108	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively,
109	with numbers.
110	
111	## From signal to lesson — the bar
112	
113	A friction signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and
114	generalizable beyond this one session.** Before adding anything:
115	
116	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded
117	  differently, even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
118	- **Route to the local pack that owns it, and prefer the strongest mechanism** — the **local
119	  promotion ladder**, at the project's own level. A project's capture surface is its **local
120	  packs** (`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/`): pick the pack whose territory the lesson belongs
121	  to, then a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in that pack's `rules` (its failure message
122	  *is* the lesson; ship it with a red-first fixture), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a
123	  **pack skill**, and only what neither can carry lands as terse **prose** in the pack's
124	  `RULES.md`. Write more checks and less prose — a check relieves every session's context
125	  completely where prose only relocates it. A gotcha tied to one call site still goes as a
126	  comment at that site (above), not into any pack. When no pack's scope fits and the lesson
127	  warrants segregation, a new local pack is a self-contained directory drop.
128	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared,
129	  cross-project canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote
130	  stage lifts it there centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever
131	  travels.
132	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or
133	  something already implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
134	
135	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
136	
137	Most sessions yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write nothing
138	rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes
139	the canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a
140	genuinely new, reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.

5	
6	# Testing practices
7	
8	Portable practices for writing tests you can actually trust — proving a test fails before relying on it, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, and how to gate a fuzzy quality metric. These are project-agnostic; a consuming repo's own test *mechanics* (runner, layout, which suites exist) stay in its own docs. (General software-engineering practices live in [the engineering-practices skill](../engineering-practices/SKILL.md); CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md).)
9	
10	- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it.
11	- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. (A hostname-apex helper passed its tests but mis-stripped `tel-aviv.gov.il` → `gov.il`; the gap only surfaced when the function was run over the actual list of existing URLs.) Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once.
12	- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
13	- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
14	- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
15	- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (A UI-snapshot coverage gate parked behavioral leaves `9.1`–`9.3`/`3.4` and an unreachable `8.6` on cases that render none of them — issue #429.)
16	- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
17	- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
18	- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
19	- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
20	- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (The SPA-render fallback's CI test renders a `data:` URL whose script fills an empty root, not a real SPA — #310.)
21	- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
22	- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
23	- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
24	- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
25	- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
26	- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
27	- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

input.body:
Part of #63 — the daily `prose-to-checks-sweep` over `.claudinite/local/packs`.

## What was convertible

One rule of the three local packs' prose passed the check-the-world test: **site-copy**'s "keep the claims that describe tracking true" carries a half that constrains a *static signature in the repo artifact* — a page may not make a **blanket** denial of tracking/analytics while the site itself ships an analytics beacon. One shipped asset loads a known analytics host, one shipped page says the site does none of it; a post-hoc scan sees the contradiction without judging anything.

This is the exact defect PR #20 shipped and review caught: Cloudflare Web Analytics added in the same commit as a `privacy.html` still leading with *"no cookies, no tracking, no personal data."*

## The check

`site-copy-analytics-claims` — **blocking**, world scope, registered on the `site-copy` pack.

Detection is **scoped, not grepped**:

- Markup, HTML comments and `<script>`/`<style>` bodies are blanked **same-length** before matching, so a denial in an attribute, a comment or a JS string is not page copy — and a match index still maps to its real source line.
- The `<meta name="description">` is read as a second copy segment: it never renders on the page but it *is* published copy (search results, link previews), and it's where a stale denial hides longest.
- Every phrase matches on **adjacent** words, so the narrower claims that stay true can never fire: *"no cross-site tracking"*, *"no advertising trackers"*, *"no cookies set by us"*, *"no personal data"*.
- `analytics-free` is negation-guarded, so the honest form — *"this site is **not** analytics-free"*, which the shipped page uses — stays quiet.
- Analytics vendors are matched as **hosts**, never product names: a page may link to `cloudflare.com/web-analytics/` while describing the tool without shipping a beacon.
- The scan is the site's own shipped assets (`.html`/`.js`/`.css`), never `.claudinite/` — the rule module itself names every host in the list.

## See-it-fail

Against the **real corpus**, not just fixtures. Re-introducing PR #20's original lede into `site/privacy.html` turns the world sweep red:

```
[BLOCKING] site-copy-analytics-claims  site/privacy.html:24
  claims "no tracking" while the site ships analytics (site/analytics.js loads cloudflareinsights.com)
  Why: a blanket "no tracking"/"no analytics" claim beside a live beacon is a false public
       statement about what the site does to its visitors, and it goes stale silently —
       the code changes, the copy does not
  Fix: say what is actually measured first, then keep only the narrower claims that stay
       true — "no cookies set by us", "no cross-site tracking", "no ads" — instead of the
       blanket "no tracking"; if the site should ship no analytics, remove the beacon
       rather than the sentence
  More: .claudinite/local/packs/site-copy/RULES.md
```

The shipped copy is green (`EXIT:0`).

The fixture suite is 9 cases — 4 firing, 5 quiet. Every guard was mutated in turn (beacon gate, `.claudinite/` exclusion, tag blanking, script-body blanking, meta segment, negation guard, wrapped-phrase matching) and a fixture bit for each one, so no case passes for free.

The repo has no test runner and no `npm test` script, so the suite is `node:test` and runs standalone:

```
node .claudinite/local/packs/site-copy/analytics-claims.test.mjs
```

## Deletion test: the prose stays whole

The `site-copy/RULES.md` paragraph is **not** deleted. The check covers only the contradiction; the paragraph also carries three things the finding's `fix` line never states:

1. the **same-commit** co-change discipline (the check catches the end state whenever it exists, not the review round-trip the rule is trying to avoid),
2. the instruction to sweep the **footer and marketing copy** that reference the privacy page, not just `privacy.html`,
3. a far wider class — *any* tracking or data-collection behaviour change, where the check only ever sees an analytics beacon against a blanket denial.

Per the skill's deletion test, a paragraph carrying something the check does not stays whole rather than being trimmed.

## Not converted, and why

- **repo-mechanics / "a step only the owner can perform goes in its own issue"** — the artifact is a PR body, which no scan over the repo tree can observe.
- **repo-mechanics / "check the canon packs before hand-authoring release or CI plumbing"** — "a sibling repo already solved this" is not a signature in this tree, and no vendored pack here declares ownership of the pipeline to compare against.
- **session-tooling (all seven rules)** — every one is about what a tool does at runtime (`WebFetch` summarizing, a `ToolSearch` miss, an `Edit` precondition, an `enable_pr_auto_merge` refusal). None leaves a static artifact behind.

## Bounded surface

The new rule module, its fixture, and the `pack.mjs` registration (plus its header comment, which claimed this pack could carry no checks at all). Nothing else touched; nothing under `.claudinite/shared/` touched.

Not auto-merged — this task's outcome ceiling is `open-pr`, and a new blocking check wants owner eyes before it can turn CI red.
